subject: Climate & Environment
title: Waterborne Diseases
description: A micro-lesson that makes Waterborne Diseases usable.

hook.text: Unsafe water kills more people than all forms of violence — including war — combined.

buildup.text: Cholera, typhoid, and dysentery spread through water contaminated with human waste.

discovery.text: Diarrheal disease kills over 500,000 children under five every year — most preventable.

twist.text: A simple water filter or chlorine tablet can eliminate over 99% of waterborne pathogens.

climax.text: Clean water and basic sanitation prevent more death than any vaccine ever invented.

punchline.text: The deadliest thing in many countries is a glass of water.

quiz.question: How many children die annually from diarrheal disease?

details.summary: Waterborne diseases including cholera, typhoid, and dysentery spread through water contaminated with human or animal waste. They kill over 1.5 million people per year, mostly children under five in developing countries, and are almost entirely preventable with clean water and basic sanitation.
details.whyItMatters: Waterborne diseases are a leading cause of child mortality in low-income countries. Investing in clean water and sanitation is one of the most cost-effective public health interventions.
takeaways: Waterborne diseases kill over 1.5 million people annually
Children under five are the most vulnerable victims
Clean water and sanitation can prevent nearly all cases

faq.question: Why does cholera still kill people in the 21st century?
faq.answer: Cholera thrives where sanitation and clean water are absent. Conflict, poverty, and natural disasters disrupt water treatment, creating outbreaks. Recent cholera surges in Yemen, Haiti, and parts of Africa show how fragile progress remains in the poorest regions.

faq.question: How much does it cost to prevent waterborne diseases?
faq.answer: The WHO estimates that every dollar spent on water and sanitation returns four dollars in reduced healthcare costs and increased productivity. Basic interventions like chlorination, household water filters, and latrines are inexpensive and highly effective.
